<dl class="radar-defs" aria-label="What each axis measures"><dt>Uneven ensembles</dt><dd>How long a batch takes when every sample stops at its own step, at N = 1,000,000.</dd><dt>Regular ensembles</dt><dd>How long a batch takes when every sample runs the same orbit, at N = 1,000,000.</dd><dt>Memory</dt><dd>Peak memory the process holds for the same workload (device memory on a GPU; host memory on a CPU, net of the benchmark harness&#x27;s control copy).</dd><dt>Code size</dt><dd>Lines of code the task takes, non-blank and non-comment.</dd><dt>Tensor workloads (qualitative)</dt><dd>Tensor workloads (qualitative): how naturally a tool expresses dense array maths (batched linear algebra, convolutions, broadcasting) and how much of it its tuned libraries cover. 5 = this is its home ground.</dd><dt>Array-style programming (qualitative)</dt><dd>Array-style programming (qualitative): how naturally you write whole-array expressions eagerly, the NumPy way. 5 = the array expression is the programming model. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Half precision and below (qualitative)</dt><dd>Half precision and below (qualitative): FP16, BF16, FP8 and FP4 arithmetic and tensor cores (FP32 and FP64 are measured on the other axes). 5 = these formats and tensor cores are first-class paths. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Single-thread abstraction (qualitative)</dt><dd>Single-thread abstraction (qualitative): how fully you can write the code for one sample, one step, and let the tool run it over the batch: threads, launches, early stopping and scheduling included. 5 = you write one sample and nothing else. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Differentiable kernels (qualitative)</dt><dd>Differentiable kernels (qualitative): how directly you get forward- and reverse-mode derivatives of your own kernels, on GPU and on CPU. 5 = built in for every kernel written in the tool&#x27;s own vocabulary.</dd><dt>Low-level control (qualitative)</dt><dd>Low-level control (qualitative): how much of the GPU&#x27;s execution you control from the tool&#x27;s own language: thread indexing, shared memory, atomics, launch shape, synchronisation (raw CUDA/C++ not counted). 5 = you write what each thread does and how it is launched. On a CPU the same question is asked of threads, SIMD and memory layout. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Works with your arrays (qualitative)</dt><dd>Works with your arrays (qualitative): how freely arrays move to and from other frameworks without copies. 5 = zero-copy exchange is the norm.</dd><dt>Deploy outside Python (qualitative)</dt><dd>Deploy outside Python (qualitative): whether a compiled kernel can run from programs that are not Python. 5 = a compiled artefact any program can load.</dd><dt>Extensibility (qualitative)</dt><dd>Extensibility (qualitative): how readily new hardware, backends and features can be added without losing speed. 5 = a documented plugin path across many targets. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd></dl>

<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-note-lead">Every measured axis is the per-sample ensemble workload raptor is built for; dense tensor maths, training and half precision are the qualitative axes, where PyTorch and JAX lead. Outer is better; overlaps are complementary, not a ranking.</p>
<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-caption-control">NVIDIA Warp gives you near-total control of every kernel, short of raw CUDA. raptor hands that control to the engine on purpose, so compaction and the launch shape are decided at run time; the two are different trade-offs, not a ranking.</p>
<details class="radar-data radar-howto"><summary>How to read this radar</summary><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each of the six majors is the plain mean of its minor axes (the detailed radar draws every minor), with equal weights and the same rule for every tool; a minor a tool has no reading on is left out of its mean and the major's marker is drawn hollow. Hover or tap a major to see its minors.</p><ul class="radar-howto-list radar-howto-majors"><li><strong>Ensemble speed</strong>: Uneven ensembles and Regular ensembles; measured.</li><li><strong>Footprint and turnaround</strong>: Memory and Code size; measured.</li><li><strong>Tensors and precision</strong>: Tensor workloads, Array-style programming and Half precision and below; qualitative.</li><li><strong>One-sample authoring</strong>: Single-thread abstraction and Differentiable kernels; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Low-level control</strong>: A single axis, so nothing is averaged; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Reach</strong>: Works with your arrays, Deploy outside Python and Extensibility; qualitative.</li></ul><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each measured axis is stretched over its own best-to-worst range, so ring labels differ per axis (code size: at least 4x). Axes are grouped by theme, so read the axes, not the area.</p><p class="axis-note radar-note">Italic axes are the author's judgement, not measurements: hollow markers, a linear scale, and no marker where a tool has no reading. A hollow marker on a measured axis means a minor is missing. The hover panel has each axis's full wording.</p><ul class="radar-howto-list radar-howto-anchors"><li><strong>Tensor workloads</strong>: 5 = dense array maths, batched linear algebra and convolutions are its home ground.</li><li><strong>Array-style programming</strong>: 5 = the whole-array expression is the programming model.</li><li><strong>Half precision and below</strong>: 5 = FP16, BF16, FP8, FP4 and tensor cores are first-class paths.</li><li><strong>Single-thread abstraction</strong>: 5 = you write one sample and nothing else.</li><li><strong>Differentiable kernels</strong>: 5 = derivatives are built in for every kernel written in the tool.</li><li><strong>Low-level control</strong>: 5 = you write what each thread does and how it is launched.</li><li><strong>Works with your arrays</strong>: 5 = zero-copy exchange with other frameworks is the norm.</li><li><strong>Deploy outside Python</strong>: 5 = a compiled artefact any program can load.</li><li><strong>Extensibility</strong>: 5 = a documented plugin path across many targets.</li></ul><p class="axis-note radar-note"><a href="https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html">Every number, in the full tables</a>.</p></details>

<dl class="radar-defs" aria-label="What each axis measures"><dt>Uneven ensembles</dt><dd>How long a batch takes when every sample stops at its own step, at N = 1,000,000.</dd><dt>Regular ensembles</dt><dd>How long a batch takes when every sample runs the same orbit, at N = 1,000,000.</dd><dt>Memory</dt><dd>Peak memory the process holds for the same workload (device memory on a GPU; host memory on a CPU, net of the benchmark harness&#x27;s control copy).</dd><dt>Code size</dt><dd>Lines of code the task takes, non-blank and non-comment.</dd><dt>Tensor workloads (qualitative)</dt><dd>Tensor workloads (qualitative): how naturally a tool expresses dense array maths (batched linear algebra, convolutions, broadcasting) and how much of it its tuned libraries cover. 5 = this is its home ground.</dd><dt>Array-style programming (qualitative)</dt><dd>Array-style programming (qualitative): how naturally you write whole-array expressions eagerly, the NumPy way. 5 = the array expression is the programming model. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Half precision and below (qualitative)</dt><dd>Half precision and below (qualitative): FP16, BF16, FP8 and FP4 arithmetic and tensor cores (FP32 and FP64 are measured on the other axes). 5 = these formats and tensor cores are first-class paths. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Single-thread abstraction (qualitative)</dt><dd>Single-thread abstraction (qualitative): how fully you can write the code for one sample, one step, and let the tool run it over the batch: threads, launches, early stopping and scheduling included. 5 = you write one sample and nothing else. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Differentiable kernels (qualitative)</dt><dd>Differentiable kernels (qualitative): how directly you get forward- and reverse-mode derivatives of your own kernels, on GPU and on CPU. 5 = built in for every kernel written in the tool&#x27;s own vocabulary.</dd><dt>Low-level control (qualitative)</dt><dd>Low-level control (qualitative): how much of the GPU&#x27;s execution you control from the tool&#x27;s own language: thread indexing, shared memory, atomics, launch shape, synchronisation (raw CUDA/C++ not counted). 5 = you write what each thread does and how it is launched. On a CPU the same question is asked of threads, SIMD and memory layout. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd><dt>Works with your arrays (qualitative)</dt><dd>Works with your arrays (qualitative): how freely arrays move to and from other frameworks without copies. 5 = zero-copy exchange is the norm.</dd><dt>Deploy outside Python (qualitative)</dt><dd>Deploy outside Python (qualitative): whether a compiled kernel can run from programs that are not Python. 5 = a compiled artefact any program can load.</dd><dt>Extensibility (qualitative)</dt><dd>Extensibility (qualitative): how readily new hardware, backends and features can be added without losing speed. 5 = a documented plugin path across many targets. Scores are the author&#x27;s judgement.</dd></dl>

<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-note-lead">Every measured axis is the per-sample ensemble workload raptor is built for; dense tensor maths, training and half precision are the qualitative axes, where PyTorch and JAX lead. Outer is better; overlaps are complementary, not a ranking.</p>
<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-caption-control">NVIDIA Warp gives you near-total control of every kernel, short of raw CUDA. raptor hands that control to the engine on purpose, so compaction and the launch shape are decided at run time; the two are different trade-offs, not a ranking.</p>
<details class="radar-data radar-howto"><summary>How to read this radar</summary><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each of the six majors is the plain mean of its minor axes (the detailed radar draws every minor), with equal weights and the same rule for every tool; a minor a tool has no reading on is left out of its mean and the major's marker is drawn hollow. Hover or tap a major to see its minors.</p><ul class="radar-howto-list radar-howto-majors"><li><strong>Ensemble speed</strong>: Uneven ensembles and Regular ensembles; measured.</li><li><strong>Footprint and turnaround</strong>: Memory and Code size; measured.</li><li><strong>Tensors and precision</strong>: Tensor workloads, Array-style programming and Half precision and below; qualitative.</li><li><strong>One-sample authoring</strong>: Single-thread abstraction and Differentiable kernels; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Low-level control</strong>: A single axis, so nothing is averaged; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Reach</strong>: Works with your arrays, Deploy outside Python and Extensibility; qualitative.</li></ul><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each measured axis is stretched over its own best-to-worst range, so ring labels differ per axis (code size: at least 4x). Axes are grouped by theme, so read the axes, not the area.</p><p class="axis-note radar-note">Italic axes are the author's judgement, not measurements: hollow markers, a linear scale, and no marker where a tool has no reading. A hollow marker on a measured axis means a minor is missing. The hover panel has each axis's full wording.</p><ul class="radar-howto-list radar-howto-anchors"><li><strong>Tensor workloads</strong>: 5 = dense array maths, batched linear algebra and convolutions are its home ground.</li><li><strong>Array-style programming</strong>: 5 = the whole-array expression is the programming model.</li><li><strong>Half precision and below</strong>: 5 = FP16, BF16, FP8, FP4 and tensor cores are first-class paths.</li><li><strong>Single-thread abstraction</strong>: 5 = you write one sample and nothing else.</li><li><strong>Differentiable kernels</strong>: 5 = derivatives are built in for every kernel written in the tool.</li><li><strong>Low-level control</strong>: 5 = you write what each thread does and how it is launched.</li><li><strong>Works with your arrays</strong>: 5 = zero-copy exchange with other frameworks is the norm.</li><li><strong>Deploy outside Python</strong>: 5 = a compiled artefact any program can load.</li><li><strong>Extensibility</strong>: 5 = a documented plugin path across many targets.</li></ul><p class="axis-note radar-note"><a href="https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html">Every number, in the full tables</a>.</p></details>
